cards.title: Old certainties, quietly retired
cards.body: Three pieces today quietly retire ideas about the mind that you were probably taught as fact: that a "lizard brain" runs your fear, that the brain works like a digital computer, that reading is something we were built to do. The one not to miss is the piece on the man who lost his amygdala — the lizard-brain story, it turns out, was never really in the evidence. The rest of the deck sits lighter: zero before it became a number, why onion prices swing, and day three of the book.

cards.title: New theory: the brain computes with waves, not circuits
cards.body: Three MIT scientists argue the brain is not a digital machine flipping switches one step at a time. It is closer to an analog one: rhythms that overlap, add and cancel, doing many calculations at once. Consciousness appears, they say, when those rhythms pull the whole brain into one organized state. This is a theory, not a measurement.

sections.text:
Someone tosses you a set of keys without warning. You catch them. In that half second your brain pulled together memory, aim and a plan — far faster than its wiring could have changed.

For decades the working picture of the brain has been a circuit board. Neurons meet at junctions called synapses, and the strength of those junctions holds what you know. The picture is comfortable because it matches the machine on your desk: a digital computer works through switches and gates, one step at a time.

Earl Miller and two colleagues at MIT say that picture is not wrong, only unfinished. Their theory in The Journal of Neuroscience starts from two awkward facts. First, changing a synapse is chemistry, and chemistry is slow — too slow for a world that throws something new at you every second. Second, most neurons do not hold one job. A single cell answers to several different cues and situations, joining many networks at the same time. They call this mixed selectivity. It buys the brain huge power, but it leaves a question: with all those networks overlapping, what decides which one is running now?

Their answer is brain waves. A brain wave is just large groups of neurons firing in a shared rhythm, rising and falling together. Slow rhythms, called alpha and beta, carry your memories and your goals. Faster ones, called gamma, carry what your senses report this instant. The slow waves control the fast ones. Synapses store the material; the waves decide which material is live.

This is where analog comes in. A digital circuit gets its answer by stepping: switch, gate, switch. Waves do not step. Drop two stones in a pond and watch the ripples cross. Where two high points meet, the water rises. Where a high point meets a low one, it flattens. Nobody computed that sum. It happened everywhere at once, because that is what waves physically do. In the cortex — the brain's outer layer — waves meet the same way, adding and subtracting, running many calculations at once. "The brain exploits its own physics," the authors write.

The slow waves come with an address. They act on particular patches of cortex and travel across it, setting where and when gamma waves may handle incoming information, and which neurons take part — beta acting as a "mobile stencil". The traffic runs both ways: waves rise out of neurons firing, and the electric field they make reaches back and nudges that firing, very fast.

Consciousness, in this theory, is what appears when these wave patterns pull the whole cortex into one organized, connected state. The strongest support so far comes from anesthesia. Miller and his colleague Emery Brown have shown that three drugs with three different molecular mechanisms all switch a person off the same way — by breaking up wave dynamics. Being awake, they argue, depends less on which receptors or cell types are involved than on whether the large-scale wave order holds.

The swap has a practical payoff. If thought lives in wiring, treating it means reaching the wiring. If thought lives in rhythms, you have a target you can push on from outside the skull, without surgery. That is why Miller's lab now studies waves in autism, and why he calls treatment built on wave dynamics an obligation, not an opportunity.

sections.label: Key takeaways
items: Then: the brain as circuit board — what you know held in synapses, thinking as steps through wiring.
Now: synapses still store, but waves decide what is active, where and when — fast enough to improvise.
Analog means the sums happen by themselves where waves overlap, many at once, instead of one step at a time.
Consciousness becomes a question of wave order, not particular receptors — which is why three unrelated anesthetics produce the same blank.

sections.label: The caveat
sections.text: This is a theory, not a finding. The paper is an argument built from years of existing experiments — mixed selectivity, slow waves controlling fast ones, the anesthesia work — not a new result. The central claim, that the brain really is doing analog computation, has not been seen directly. Miller says so plainly: the next step is to look for signs of analog computation in brain wave patterns. Until that arrives, this is the most interesting guess available, not settled ground.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: The physics was already there, humming inside the skull. It would be strange if evolution had left it unspent.

recall.q: What does "analog" mean in this theory — what do waves do that switches and gates don't?
recall.a: Where waves overlap, they add and subtract on their own, so many calculations happen at once across space instead of one step at a time. The brain gets that arithmetic free from its own physics.

cards.title: Zero was a bookkeeping mark before it became a number
cards.body: Zero began in Mesopotamia as punctuation: a wedge meaning 'nothing in this column'. It only held the other digits in place. India turned that empty place into an empty number — one you can add and multiply. In Robert Kaplan's telling, the hinge is a Sanskrit word for 'place'.

sections.text:
A scribe at Kish, in Mesopotamia, wrote his zeroes as three small hooks. Another scribe of the same period — maybe as early as 700 BCE — used one hook, so his zeroes look exactly like his tens. Kaplan reads that mess as youth: we are near the start of something when nobody has agreed what it looks like.

His book The Nothing That Is follows one long promotion. Zero starts as bookkeeping punctuation, a mark that holds a column open. It ends as a number you can add, subtract and multiply like any other. Everything between is the story.

Around 3000 BCE in Sumer — now Iraq — people counted by 1s and 10s, and also by 60s. The 60s probably came from matching their own weights against another culture's, and we still live inside them: sixty minutes in an hour, 360 degrees in a circle. Mixed bases make a mess. By 2000 BCE the Sumerian system — triangular marks cut into wet clay — was clumsy enough to need a fix.

The fix came in the middle of the first millennium BCE. Some scribe found a way to wedge the accounting columns apart, so a reader could see that this column held nothing. That is the idea of zero without a symbol for it. It is not a number yet. It is a gap-keeper, something you put between digits so they land in the right places.

Greece came at it from the other side. Archimedes needed names for quantities past the myriad — ten thousand, the largest Greek number-name. He built a system of orders that climbs toward huge numbers in stages. He came close to inventing powers. He never invented zero, and no Greek word for it exists: names belong to things, and zero is a no-thing that counts what isn't there.

India is where the promotion happens. The mathematician and astronomer Āryabhata wanted a compact way to store big numbers, so he built nonsense words — consonants for digits, vowels for places — in which 386 comes out as CASAGI. The scheme gave him nine places; as an astronomer he needed more, so he doubled the vowels to reach eighteen. There is no zero anywhere in it. But his word for place is kha, and kha later becomes one of the most common Indian words for zero.

That is the shift caught mid-motion: an empty place where a digit can sit becomes an empty number that nudges the other digits along. The oldest zero symbol we still have is Indian too — a stone tablet from 876 CE recording a garden of 270 by 50, written as 27° and 5°. Copper plates three centuries older carry the same small circle, but eleventh-century India was full of fakes, so nobody can prove they are real.

What hung in the balance, Kaplan says, was whether zero would be "the mark of the empty, or the empty mark" — the absence of any number, or a number for that absence. The first leaves zero outside mathematics, scenery the numbers pass through. The second seats it among them. The second is the one that reached us, and the 1s and 0s on this screen are what it grew into.

sections.label: Key takeaways
items: Sumer counted in 1s, 10s and 60s at once. The mixed bases made numbers messy — and we still live in the 60s: sixty minutes in an hour, 360 degrees in a circle.
The Greeks built ladders toward the very large but never named its opposite. Naming was the block: zero names no thing.
India holds the oldest zero symbol we still have — a stone from 876 CE recording a garden of 270 by 50.
Āryabhata's word for place, kha, became a common Indian word for zero — one idea changing meaning inside a single syllable.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: Zero had to be somewhere before it could be something.

recall.q: Mesopotamian scribes were using a zero sign more than a thousand years before India. So what did India actually add?
recall.a: Mesopotamia had a placeholder — a mark meaning 'this column is empty', useful only for holding the other digits in position. India turned that empty place into an empty number, a number like any other. The trace is Āryabhata's word for place, kha, which later came to mean zero.

cards.title: Day 3 · Twice two makes five
cards.body: The case against the Palace of Crystal reaches its peak today — and then the arguer takes the whole thing back. What survives the retraction is the thing this book has been circling all along: a memory, and the wet snow.

sections.text:
Free will trained to coincide with arithmetic is not free will. Twice two makes four whether you consent or not — so what, he asks, is left to want?

Then he backs off: he is joking, his jokes aren't brilliant, he is "jesting against the grain." The retreat is tactical. From it he flips the burden of proof — you want to reform man's will by science, but how do you know his inclinations need reforming, or that it would benefit him? "It may be the law of logic, but not the law of humanity."

Then he grants their premise so completely it breaks in his hands. Man is a creative animal, an engineer, made "incessantly and eternally to make new roads, wherever they may lead." So why does he love destruction and chaos too? Because "he is instinctively afraid of attaining his object and completing the edifice he is constructing." He loves the building from a distance, wants to build it rather than live in it, and leaves it when finished to les animaux domestiques — the ants, the sheep, whose ant-heap endures forever. Man is a chess player who loves the game, not the end of it.

That is the day's real thesis, and it isn't a joke: perhaps the only goal is the process of attaining, "in life itself, and not in the thing to be attained." Anything attained hardens into a formula, "and such positiveness is not life, gentlemen, but is the beginning of death." So man crosses oceans hunting mathematical certainty and dreads finding it, because "when he has found it there will be nothing for him to look for." Workmen at least finish, get paid, go to the tavern, get taken to the police-station — occupation for a week. "But where can man go?"

Patience gone, the argument turns to abuse: twice two makes four is "a pert coxcomb who stands with arms akimbo barring your path and spitting." And he offers his counter-currency, twice two makes five.

Then the turn that undoes his own opening. Perhaps man loves suffering as much as well-being — don't consult history, "only ask yourself, if you are a man and have lived at all." He takes neither side: he holds no brief for suffering or well-being, only "for my caprice, and for its being guaranteed to me when necessary." Suffering is unthinkable in the crystal palace because suffering means doubt. And then, quietly: "suffering is the sole origin of consciousness." The disease he began by cursing is the one thing he would never trade.

Chapter X names what he is actually refusing. He'd crawl into a hen-house to stay dry but won't call it a palace out of gratitude. The palace's crime is that it can never be destroyed and you cannot put your tongue out at it, even on the sly — and he insists it isn't that he enjoys the gesture. What he resents is that nobody has built the thing he wouldn't want to mock. "Destroy my desires, eradicate my ideals, show me something better, and I will follow you." Until then, not one brick.

Then he detonates the structure himself. "Hurrah for underground!" — and instantly, "even now I am lying!" It isn't underground he wants but "something different, quite different, for which I am thirsting, but which I cannot find." He believes not one word he has written; he is "lying like a cobbler." He then writes out his readers' contempt for him — you have no respect for your own suffering, you hide your last word from fear — and admits he invented that too, after forty years listening through a crack under the floor.

What survives, once the argument is confessed as bluff, is memory. He wants to test whether a man can be open even with himself. Heine says true autobiography is impossible and Rousseau lied from vanity; he agrees, and starts anyway. One memory haunts him "like an annoying tune that one cannot get rid of." Snow is falling, yellow and dingy.

Part II. He is twenty-four, in the office, unable to hold anyone's gaze. The mechanism is exact: out of "unbounded vanity" and an impossible standard he looks at himself with loathing — hating his face, willing to look base if only he could look intelligent — and then reads that loathing on every face around him.

sections.label: From the book
sections.text: Every man has reminiscences which he would not tell to everyone, but only to his friends. He has other matters in his mind which he would not reveal even to his friends, but only to himself, and that in secret. But there are other things which a man is afraid to tell even to himself, and every decent man has a number of such things stored away in his mind. The more decent he is, the greater the number of such things in his mind.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: He loves the process of attaining, but does not quite like to have attained.

recall.q: Why does he think man loves destruction and chaos as much as he loves building?
recall.a: Because man is afraid of finishing. He loves the edifice from a distance and doesn't want to live in it — the goal is "the incessant process of attaining," life itself, since anything attained hardens into a formula as positive as twice two, and "such positiveness is not life... but is the beginning of death."

cards.attribution: Fyodor Dostoyevsky · Constance Garnett tr. · public domain

cards.title: Aristotle's vegetable: the mind that stops checking itself
cards.body: Aristotle said nobody can truly believe a thing and its opposite at once. What he proved is smaller: such a person cannot defend himself. He can still exist. That gap is where Orwell's doublethink lives — and we now walk into it out of tiredness.

sections.text: Aristotle is arguing with someone who will not argue back. In Book Four of the Metaphysics he defends the most basic rule in logic — a thing cannot both be and not be. Then he meets a man who refuses to settle: something is so, and also not so, and he does not mind. Aristotle asks what is left to separate him from the vegetables. It sounds like an insult. It is a description.

sections.label: The passage
sections.text:
Aristotle states the rule twice.

About the world: the same attribute cannot at the same time belong and not belong to the same subject in the same respect.

About minds: it is impossible for anyone to believe the same thing to be and not to be.

And of the man who seems to manage it anyway: what remains to distinguish him from the vegetables?

Take the first line. It is about the world, not about you: nothing can have and lack the same quality at the same moment, in the same way. Aristotle calls this the firmest principle there is — and refuses to prove it. Any proof would have to use it. The argument would go in a circle before it began.

So he does something else. He asks the man who denies the rule to do one thing: say something that means something. That is harder than it sounds. To mean this is to not mean that. If your word picks out one thing rather than another, you have already used the rule. He is beaten by opening his mouth.

The second line looks the same. It is not. It is about minds: nobody can really believe a thing and its opposite. The trap does not reach that far. It shows that denying the rule cannot be defended. It does not show that nobody can live inside a contradiction. Aristotle treats the two as one because he assumes that anyone who can speak wants to be defensible — that wanting your beliefs to agree comes free with thinking. Drop that assumption and the vegetable is no longer the far edge of being human. It becomes a place a person can arrive at.

That is Orwell's point. Doublethink is not ordinary confusion. Everyone holds beliefs that clash. We notice, we squirm, we fix one. That order is reason working, not failing. Doublethink keeps the noticing and drops the squirm and the fix. The clash is seen, seen clearly as a clash, and nothing follows.

So what is given up is not logic. It is a demand: that your beliefs answer to each other. That demand sits above every single belief, so evidence cannot reach it. A false belief can be corrected. A person who no longer feels a clash as a cost gives the correction nothing to hold.

Hannah Arendt described the ideal subject of a total regime: not someone convinced by lies, but someone for whom the difference between true and false has stopped mattering. Harry Frankfurt found the same person with no regime at all. A liar still tracks the truth, so he can steer around it. The one who does not care where the truth is has left the game.

Endless clashing claims ask a checking mind for a debt it cannot pay. So it goes unpaid — from tiredness, not from a decision. Nobody gives up consistency. They stop having time for it, and the loss never announces itself. Which is why more facts do not help. A correction only works on someone who would be embarrassed by it.

sections.label: See it in your life
items: Two headlines that cannot both be true scroll past. You feel nothing. You keep going. That flat feeling is the debt going unpaid.
You catch yourself holding two beliefs that clash, and a small discomfort follows. That discomfort is not a flaw. It is the part doing the work — and the part doublethink deletes.
Someone corrects you. You accept it. Nothing in you moves. The correction lands with the same flatness as the error it replaced.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: What defines a mind is not what it believes. It is whether it still tests what it believes. The first changes all the time. The second, once let go, is the hardest thing to get back.

recall.q: Aristotle showed that the man who denies the rule cannot defend himself. What did he fail to show — and why does that gap matter?
recall.a: He failed to show that nobody can live inside a contradiction. Being unable to defend a position and being unable to hold one are different things. Drop his assumption that a thinking being wants to be defensible, and the vegetable is not an impossible edge case. It is somewhere a mind can end up.

cards.title: Why the chatbot's one clean answer feels true
cards.body: A chatbot's reply is the easiest thing you will read all day, and easy things feel true. So your certainty goes up while the evidence stays exactly where it was.

sections.text:
Take a true sentence and print it in a colour that is slightly hard to read. People rate it as less likely to be true. Print it in crisp black and they trust it more. Nothing about the sentence changed — only the effort of reading it.

Ali Jasemi, a psychologist who studies how people learn and stay informed online, thinks that small finding explains something large. By February this year, ChatGPT alone had 900 million weekly users, mostly asking it for information and practical advice.

sections.label: Why does one clean paragraph feel so true?
sections.text:
Two habits of mind do the work. The first is processing fluency — the easier something is to take in, the truer it feels. Decades of research sit behind it, and the colour experiment is one small corner. A chatbot reply is instant, clean and confident, so it presses that button directly.

The second is the machine heuristic — the belief that a machine wants nothing for itself. Trust in news organisations is low, partly because people suspect a motive behind the story. A chatbot answer has no author, so there is no one to suspect.

sections.label: What is the chatbot doing to earn that?
sections.text:
It hides the argument. Books, newspapers and people used to disagree with each other, and your judgment formed in the gaps between them. Search engines kept part of that: a list of links still showed you the answer had rivals. A chatbot returns one paragraph, and the rivals are gone.

That absence is comfortable, and the comfort is the trap. In experiments, people were too sure when they got one answer and not sure enough when they got several — even when the several were more accurate. Sources that clash also help you remember where each fact came from. Sources that agree do not. Ten sources become one paragraph, and the disagreement leaves your view, not the world.

sections.label: When should I not trust it?
sections.text:
More often than feels possible. The largest study of its kind — run by the European Broadcasting Union, led by the BBC, across 18 countries and 14 languages — found that almost half of AI assistants' news answers had at least one serious problem. Bad sourcing was the most common fault. Others were misleading, out of date, missing a key detail, or simply made up.

Almost nobody catches it. Pew tracked what people actually do in their browsers: when Google shows an AI summary, readers open a source on 8% of visits, against 15% when it does not. They click the links inside the summary 1% of the time.

sections.label: What does using one wisely look like?
sections.text: Jasemi does not ask you to stop. Telling people to drop one of the handiest tools ever built works about as well as telling them to swap cars for horses. He asks you to add one deliberate habit to an automatic one. Notice the pull first. Then treat the reply as a starting point, not the final word: ask for the sources, open them, and look for the view that disagrees.

sections.label: The question nobody can answer yet
sections.text: Jasemi's honest answer is that he does not know what this does to a whole society. The 2026 Reuters Institute report finds 10% of people worldwide now use a chatbot for news each week, rising to 16% among the under-35s. Only 42% of them say they usually check the links. An audience that is misinformed is also an audience that votes. What that does over years, no psychologist can tell you yet.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: Certainty built from seeing less is not knowledge. It only feels the same.

recall.q: Ten sources disagree. A chatbot turns them into one paragraph. Why does the reader end up more certain than before?
recall.a: Because the disagreement is what would normally slow you down and make you check. Hiding it does not improve the answer — it removes the friction. In experiments, people were too sure when they got one answer and not sure enough when they got several, even when the several were more accurate.

cards.title: Why India's onion prices swing: the cobweb cycle
cards.body: An onion farmer picks how much to plant months before the crop can be sold. The only price to plant against is last year's. That one lag is enough to swing prices hard, with no bad weather needed.

sections.text:
Walk it one step at a time. Prices crash after a heavy harvest, so farmers plant less. The thin crop becomes a shortage and prices soar — onions have crossed ₹60 a kg in much of India, and the government is moving reserve stock on a freight train it calls the "Kanda Express". Farmers see those prices and rush to plant. Everyone plants at once, supply floods in, prices crash, and the loop restarts.

Economists named this the cobweb cycle in the 1930s — Nicholas Kaldor and Jan Tinbergen among them — after the shape supply and price trace on a graph. Any crop with a long gap between the planting decision and the sale can run it.

Stored onions would soften the swing, but only the rabi crop keeps well, and much of it rots in open sheds. Onions have no minimum support price and no working futures market, so last year's price stays the only signal a farmer has.

sections.label: The numbers
items: ₹60 a kg — onion prices across much of India now
70% — share of India's onion output from the rabi crop, the only harvest that stores reasonably well
3 crore vs 2 crore metric tonnes — yearly production against household consumption plus exports
₹34 to ₹80 — what the farmer got versus what the shopper paid, in one case studied by the Competition Commission of India

sections.label: Why it matters
sections.text: Weather, hoarding and middlemen are real causes, but partial ones. India grows more onions than it eats and exports, yet the shortages keep coming. Buffer trains and reactive price support treat each spike after it lands. They do nothing about the decision loop that builds the next one.

sections.label: Watch next
sections.text: Onion futures — deals that fix a price today for a crop sold later. NCDEX, India's commodity derivatives exchange, got approval to launch them years ago and never really did. Onions are hard to store, and an essential vegetable is politically risky to trade. Angry voters remember the last price rise.

recall.q: Onion prices can swing wildly even in a year with normal weather. What produces the swing?
recall.a: The time lag between planting and selling. A farmer commits land months ahead with only last year's price to go on. So a crash makes everyone plant less, which creates a shortage; the high prices that follow make everyone plant more, which creates a glut. That self-repeating loop is the cobweb cycle.

cards.title: Should surgeons remove the amygdala to end fear?
cards.body: A brain tumour cost one man his right amygdala — the brain's alarm bell. His depression lifted, his gut-level fear vanished, and he now says surgeons should offer the same operation to people whose fear is ruining them. The strongest objection is not disgust at the idea. It is that the man reporting the result no longer has the part that would notice what he lost.

sections.text:
Minutes before an operation he had worked out had a six percent chance of killing him, Daniel Böttger refused the sedative. German rules let a patient refuse if he can show he is still thinking clearly. So he recited a poem he had written for the doctor who would put him under. It rhymed, it kept its beat, and it explained that he had felt no fear since surgeons took his amygdala.

The amygdala is a small part deep inside each half of the brain. It is the alarm bell: it fires the fight-or-flight rush. In 2024, surgeons cut a fist-sized tumour out of Böttger's brain, and his right amygdala came out with it. He has been, by his own account, extremely well ever since. So: should anyone choose this?

Take the yes case at full strength. His major depression — held down for years by the highest dose of an antidepressant — simply ended. He stopped the drug twice, once all at once with no step-down, and stayed fine. The gut-drop kind of fear is gone, and with it the loops of worrying about worrying, which he says need amygdala boosts to keep going. He still weighs risk and still avoids danger; that work belongs to the neocortex, the thinking outer layer, not the alarm bell. He feels pain but rarely gets stuck on it. The amygdala appears to help cause PTSD and runs hot in some other conditions, so it is not a wild target. And the modern operation is nothing like the lobotomies of the 1950s. Stereotactic radiosurgery sends many weak radiation beams through healthy tissue from different angles; only where they cross does the dose become strong enough to destroy. One procedure, he argues, against a lifetime of drugs and therapy that work less well and cost more.

Now the no case, also at full strength. Much of it comes from him. Friends told him he had changed, and some liked him less. He cannot read faces well. He fails to comfort people who are frightened. Noise now bothers him. His doctors filed this under organic personality disorder, and he grants it looks like the autism-like pattern seen after brain injury. He also lost the stick half of motivation: the fear of failing that many people run on. And he notes something sharper. Someone in hospitality or care work — or anyone in a low-trust place, where having no suspicion gets you used — could be badly damaged by this surgery and still feel wonderful about it. The feeling and the outcome come apart. Nobody can put an amygdala back.

So what would settle it? Not a better first-person account. It needs outcomes judged from outside the patient — jobs held, relationships kept, harm avoided — in people whose amygdala is already wrecking their lives, tracked for years and set against the treatments they would have had instead. Böttger's own case cannot supply that. He is one man. The same operation took part of his hippocampus and temporal cortex, so cause and effect are tangled. And the person rating the loss is the person whose loss-detector was removed.

The balance is not even. One vivid, well-argued case report is nowhere near enough to offer this to healthy people. But it is enough to say that people with severe, amygdala-driven suffering deserve real trials — because the reason every surgeon he asked said no was not data. It was the memory of lobotomies.

sections.label: The caveat
sections.text: This is one man writing about himself in an essay, not a study. The same surgery removed part of his hippocampus and temporal cortex, which he says left lasting trouble with memory and finding his way — so neither the gains nor the costs can be pinned on the amygdala alone. His reported seven-point IQ rise is still awaiting a retest, and the earlier score was measured while he had cancer, depression, untreated epilepsy, test anxiety and daily medication.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: An operation that removes your alarm bell also removes the thing that would tell you it was a mistake.

recall.q: Böttger says the surgery went well by every measure he can feel. Why doesn't that settle whether amygdala removal should be offered?
recall.a: Because the operation removed the very part that would register the cost — he points out that someone could be harmed by it and still feel wonderful. Settling it needs outcomes judged from outside the patient, like work and relationships, tracked over years.

cards.title: On consciousness, every available answer is bizarre
cards.body: Eric Schwitzgebel's guiding claim: on the deepest questions about mind and universe, something bizarre must be true, and we cannot tell which. Common sense fails here. So do science and philosophy.

sections.text:
Two bodies are identical, atom for atom. Both are writhing. Both make the same sounds of protest. On one serious theory of pain, only one of them is actually in pain.

That is the sort of room the philosopher Eric Schwitzgebel keeps walking you into. He wrote a short summary of his own 2024 book, The Weirdness of the World, for people who will never open it. It runs as a set of hard questions.

sections.label: What does he mean by weird?
sections.text:
Two things at once. Bizarre: the answer badly breaks ordinary common sense. Dubious: we have no good reason to pick it over its rivals.

Quantum mechanics shows the shape of the problem. Many-worlds says reality is always splitting into near-copies of itself. Some versions of the Copenhagen view say a human observation is what makes many possibilities settle into one outcome. Bohmian mechanics and objective collapse are other options. Every one is strange, none is decided, and any new option will probably be strange too.

sections.label: Isn't plain materialism the safe choice?
sections.text:
Materialism is the view that everything, minds included, is physical stuff. Schwitzgebel thinks people miss how odd it gets.

Take pain. If pain needs a brain of our physical type, then an alien built differently can never hurt, however it behaves. If pain is instead just the right pattern of inputs and outputs, then a huge machine of beer cans and wire could hurt. Escape both by appealing to what is typical, or to evolutionary history, and you land in the opening scene: two identical bodies, writhing alike, one in pain and one not.

Group minds bite the same way. The United States, treated as a real object with people as its parts, has the features materialists point to in brains: heavy information flow inside it, a picture of itself, learning, action, a boundary it keeps up. Materialists can block the conclusion, but every block costs something else. He does not claim your country is conscious. He claims something has to give.

sections.label: Then are souls the answer?
sections.text:
Dualism says the mind is a separate thing, not made of matter. Ask which creatures get one, and four bad doors open. Only humans, and dogs and apes feel nothing at all. Every organism, and bacteria and slime moulds are conscious. A sharp line somewhere in between, except that life shades from one form to the next with no place to cut. Or partial souls, and nobody has made sense of a frog with sixty percent of a soul.

In the whole history of philosophy, East and West, no one has produced an account of mind and body that keeps common sense whole. Even Thomas Reid, the common sense philosopher, held that physical objects need immaterial souls to hold their shapes. The likeliest explanation, Schwitzgebel says, is that our common sense beliefs about mind and body simply do not fit together.

sections.label: Why can't science just settle it?
sections.text:
There is no meter you can point at a creature and read consciousness off it. To build a general theory of animal consciousness, you must first assume how common consciousness is: rare, only clever mammals and birds, or everywhere, down to insects, worms and oysters. That starting assumption shapes the theory. Someone who starts elsewhere has no reason to move.

Cosmology widens the gap. If we live in a computer simulation, the physical world may be only how the machine underneath shows itself to us. If the universe is infinite, its laws may run differently in other regions, and materialism could be a local accident rather than a deep truth. We have seen a sliver of reality: fleas on a dog, watching one hair grow, announcing how the universe works.

sections.label: How weird is he willing to get?
sections.text:
Very. One chapter builds a how-could-this-work story for Kant's transcendental idealism, the view that space depends on our minds and that things as they are in themselves stay unknowable. Suppose we are AIs inside a simulation whose computer is not material at all, but the mind of an angel. Space would then be our way of making sense of that mind's structure. He does not think it is likely. He thinks that once you can picture it, you can see how something stranger still might be true.

Another chapter argues that long after the universe cools, chance will eventually assemble a copy of your brain, and that raising your hand right now helps decide which copy appears.

sections.label: Could you be wrong about being awake?
sections.text:
Slightly, yes. People judge themselves awake while dreaming. False awakenings happen. Some leading theories say dream experience can feel exactly like waking experience. He grants maybe a twenty percent chance that he sometimes has, while asleep, experiences much like this one, plus a false sense of being awake.

So his confidence that he is awake now is about 99.9 percent, not total. He calls the stance one percent skepticism: a small but real credence, credence meaning how much belief you place in a claim, that some wildly skeptical scenario is true. It is not idle. When a short-term gain and a long-term gain sit almost exactly level, one percent skepticism tips you toward the short one.

sections.label: Does any of this matter yet?
sections.text:
It matters most for machines. We will likely soon build AI systems that some plausible theories count as richly conscious as an adult human, and other plausible theories count as no more conscious than a toaster. Their moral standing would then be genuinely undecidable. He calls them "debatable persons".

Every way of treating them is bad. Deny them rights they might deserve, and we risk slavery and murder at scale. Grant them human rights, citizenship, property, reproduction, the vote, and we risk giving up real human lives for beings with no interests worth the cost. Limited rights are safer for us and oppressive if the entities are people. His only clean answer is to refuse the situation: do not build minds whose standing is unclear. Build well below the line, or well above it and grant what is owed. Nobody can yet say where that line is, and the building has started.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: "Bags of mostly water" that can ask what the universe is made of, and admit they do not know: that is the achievement, not the answer.

recall.q: Schwitzgebel calls every serious answer here both bizarre and dubious. What does each word mean, and why does he need both?
recall.a: Bizarre means the answer breaks ordinary common sense. Dubious means we have no good grounds to prefer it over its rivals. Together they trap us: something strange must be true, and nothing available tells us which strange thing it is.

cards.title: Men's faces are wider — but not in the way science claimed
cards.body: For years, one face measurement was read as a male signal of aggression: the facial width-to-height ratio. Across 1,949 faces, men and women do not differ on it. Women's came out a shade larger — well inside the wobble a camera lens adds. Plain cheekbone width, though, separates the sexes almost perfectly.
cards.evidence: one paper, two analyses · n=1,949 lab photos (305 body-scanned) · mostly young Western adults

sections.text:
Picture two men, side by side. One has a wide face: cheekbones set far apart, a squarish look. The other's face is narrow. Guess which one is more aggressive.

For years, a large body of research said the wide one. The measure behind it is the facial width-to-height ratio — the distance between the cheekbones divided by the height of the face. It got huge attention. Men's faces were said to be proportionally wider than women's, and that shape was read as a signal built by evolution: a face that warns you its owner can fight.

A team led by Alex L. Jones at Swansea University went looking for the ground under that claim. Not fights — the sex difference itself. If men's faces are not proportionally wider, the signal has nothing to stand on.

Two problems had been sitting inside the old work. First, body size. Body parts grow with the body carrying them; researchers call this allometry. Men are usually taller and heavier, so a wider male face may only be a side effect of being bigger. Second, nobody agreed where a face ends. Width was always cheekbone to cheekbone. But some measured height from the upper lip to the brow, others from the chin to the bridge of the nose. Different rulers, different answers.

Jones's team closed both gaps across 1,949 lab photographs. They worked out all five versions of the ratio, adjusted for each person's measured height and weight, and set a bar for what counts as real: the difference had to be bigger than the distortion a camera lens makes when the zoom changes. Smaller than the wobble a lens adds, and it is not a fact about faces.

The gap between men and women fell entirely inside that wobble — and women's ratios came out slightly larger. The ratio did move with the body, though: taller people had smaller ratios, heavier people larger ones. That is the sting. Older work tying wide faces to aggression may have been tracking body weight all along.

So the team dropped the ratio and measured one thing: the raw distance between the cheekbones. The difference is huge. After adjusting for height, weight, and even shoulder width, chest size and bicep size, a man is almost certain to have a wider face than a woman of the same body size.

A ratio hides two numbers inside one. Divide a real difference by the wrong thing and it vanishes on paper while sitting right there on the face.

sections.label: The experiment
sections.text:
1,949 photographs of men and women from Western societies, all shot in a lab: facing the camera, neutral expression. Software mapped 68 points on each face.

The analysis used a Bayesian model — a method that folds in what earlier research already found and returns how probable a hypothesis is, instead of a yes-or-no verdict from one dataset. A smaller group of 305 people had been measured with 3D body scanners, which let the team subtract upper-body size as well.

sections.label: The caveat
sections.text:
One paper, one kind of image. The faces are mostly young adults from Western samples. Face structure changes over a life, and ethnic differences could shift these numbers.

Still photographs also capture only fixed bone. Real judgements of threat happen in motion — moving muscles, expressions, tone of voice. None of that is in the dataset.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: Before you trust a number about people, ask what it was divided by.

recall.q: The study found no sex difference in the facial width-to-height ratio, yet a huge sex difference in faces. How can both be true?
recall.a: The ratio divides cheekbone width by face height. Men's faces are far wider in raw terms — even after adjusting for height, weight and upper-body size — but dividing by face height cancels that difference out.

cards.title: India's industrial output is 5.6% above last year
cards.body: India's industrial production index read 125.6 in January 2023 — about 5.6% above the same month a year earlier. The index tracks output from factories, mines and power plants. It is a score, not a count: it means something only next to other months in the same series.

sections.text: The rise is not one good month. November, December and January averaged 125.4, roughly 6% above the same three months a year before. January 2023 beats every month of 2021 and every month of 2022 except one — November, at 125.8. This is the part of the economy that runs on orders, shifts and factory jobs, and it is climbing steadily, not spiking.

sections.label: The numbers
items: 125.6 — January 2023, second-highest in the series
119.0 — January 2022, the base for that 5.6% gain
101.1 — May 2021, the low point; January 2023 sits about a quarter above it
116.4 to 125.8 — October to November 2022, an 8% jump in one month

sections.label: What one month can't tell you
sections.text: One print proves little. The series swings hard — down about 4% in October 2022, up about 8% in November. The three-month average is the steadier read. And nothing in the index says what produced the gain. It counts what came out of the factories, never why.

recall.q: The January reading is 125.6 — a score with no units behind it. What makes that number mean anything, and why is a single month a weak signal?
recall.a: An index only carries meaning next to other months in the same series: 125.6 against 119.0 a year earlier is a rise of about 5.6%. One month is weak because the series swings sharply — down about 4% in October 2022, up about 8% in November. The three-month average is the steadier read.

cards.title: The extra pay for a US degree is shrinking
cards.body: For four decades, the extra pay an American college degree earned over no degree kept growing. Since 2022 it has been falling. A new paper links about 28 percent of that fall to jobs where generative AI can do part of the work — though the authors will not call AI the cause.
cards.evidence: single working paper · US Current Population Survey, Outgoing Rotation Group, through 2026 · noncausal, occupation-level

sections.text:
Guess first, and be honest. Since 2022, has the pay gap between American college graduates and everyone else grown, stayed flat, or shrunk? Almost every instinct says grown: that gap, called the college wage premium, had widened for four straight decades.

It shrank. José Azar, Mireia Gine and Javier Sanz-Espín track it in US government wage surveys, from 0.626 in 2022 to 0.575 in 2026. In the usual supply-and-demand reading, a drop that size means employers now want college workers less than before, compared with everyone else.

The authors then scored each occupation by how much of its work generative AI can do. Pay grew slowest where that score was highest, and graduates fill those jobs more than other workers do.

sections.label: The numbers
items: Wage effect of a fully AI-exposed job against an unexposed one, by 2026: −0.086
Share of the fall this explains: about 28 percent — the other roughly 72 percent is unexplained
Demand for college workers, next to everyone else: first sustained fall in a series reaching back to 1914

sections.label: Why it matters
sections.text: The authors call the pattern noncausal: they can measure it, but cannot show AI caused it. Their exposure score is attached to jobs, not people — it rates the tasks a job contains. So the data can see that pay grew slowly in AI-exposed job categories. It cannot see who actually used an AI tool, or what else hit those categories after 2022. The economist who flagged the paper does not think AI is driving these changes at all.

recall.q: The paper links AI-exposed jobs to the shrinking US college wage premium. How much of the fall does that link explain, and why won't the authors call AI the cause?
recall.a: About 28 percent, leaving roughly 72 percent unexplained. The AI exposure score is attached to occupations rather than to individual workers, so the finding is only a correlation — the authors themselves call it noncausal.

cards.title: Nahua gratitude was a debt to the dead and unborn
cards.body: Spanish friars asked a man in Texcoco for samples of polite speech. They wanted to preach better in Nahuatl. What he handed over was a system of debt: gratitude that runs back to the generations who made life workable, and forward to people not yet born. Next to that, the gratitude journal looks small.

sections.text:
Sometime between 1550 and 1570, in Texcoco, a city in the Valley of Mexico, a man sat down and wrote out polite conversation. Spanish friars were collecting this kind of material across the region. They wanted Nahuatl, the local language, so they could preach in it and convert people faster. The writer was probably a baptized Christian, and he could write in the alphabet the Spanish had brought. We know him as Pablo. Even that may be a made-up name.

What he produced is now called the Bancroft Dialogues. It has three parts. In the first, a young noblewoman stops at a relative's house on her way to the market. A trained speaker — a man whose job was formal speech — advises a newly married couple, warning them to beware "the path of the rabbit, the deer". The second part moves into the past: a bride arrives at the court of King Ixtlilxochitl, grandson of Nezahualcoyotl; a queen gives birth; the king dies, and people speak over his body. The third part returns to the present. Boys are taught how to carry themselves, and their grandmother remembers the years before the Spanish came. The boys are that dead king's direct descendants.

The friars wanted grammar. What fills page after page is thanks — and not thanks for gifts. Frances Karttunen and Camilla Townsend, whose new translation is titled How to Be Grateful, point out that Nahua gratitude stretched across generations. You repay the work of the people who came before you. You do your own duty for the people coming after, who will thank you in turn. Texcoco by then was barely holding on to the self-rule it had left. Those boys were not inheriting a kingdom. They were inheriting an account, and the speech that keeps paying it.

Now set that against how gratitude reaches us. Keep a journal. Name three good things. Say thanks before a meal, thank one loved one a day, then report whether you feel more connected. The reviewer suggests exactly this as a class exercise, and there is nothing wrong with it. But look at which way it points. It points inward. Its test is your own mood.

The Nahua version points the other way. It is owed, not felt. Much of it is owed to the dead, and to people who do not exist yet. A debt to the unborn pays back no mood at all. You pay it by doing work whose benefit lands after you. Karttunen and Townsend argue this made gratitude bigger than what we usually mean by the word — a real part of holding social life together. The harder assignment follows. Not a list of what you are thankful for, but a question: how real are your ancestors and your descendants in the choices you actually make?

sections.label: The caveat
sections.text: This is a colonial document. It was made during a conversion project, and copied later for a Jesuit grammar scholar. Christian influence shows throughout. The reviewer calls it among the best sources we have for thought close to pre-contact Nahua life — which is not the same as being it. The reviewer's own complaint is that the translators sketch this larger gratitude but never spell out what it amounts to. Take the picture across generations as an outline, not a finished theory.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: The friars asked for a language to convert people with. What Pablo handed over was a record of what the living owe.

recall.q: Nahua gratitude ran both backward and forward in time. Why does that make it impossible to treat as a mood exercise?
recall.a: Because it was owed, not felt. It ran back to the generations whose work made life workable, and forward to people not yet born. A debt to the dead and the unborn returns nothing to your mood. You can only pay it with work whose benefit arrives after you.

cards.title: Your brain has no reading part. It borrows four.
cards.body: Evolution never built a reading part — writing is far too young for that. So the brain makes one out of pieces meant for other jobs: tracking loudness, recognising faces, storing meaning. A new study of brain scans and twins suggests those starting pieces are partly inherited. The links between them are not. Those you lay down yourself, by reading.
cards.evidence: single study · Human Connectome Project scans of healthy young adults · twin comparison · correlational

sections.text:
Look at the word sitting. Nothing in your brain was built to do what just happened.

Mikael Roll, at Lund University, went looking for the parts it uses instead. He worked from detailed scans in the Human Connectome Project, a large study of healthy young adults. Nobody read inside the scanner; reading skill came from a separate test where people said written words aloud. He also compared twins who share different amounts of DNA, to see which parts were inherited.

First, sound. Before a child ever meets a letter, the brain has to hear that sitting is two pieces: sit, then ting. It does that by tracking loudness. Most syllables open quiet on a consonant (s-), swell at the vowel (-i-, the part you can sing), then fade (-t). A strip sits beside the primary auditory cortex — the brain's first stop for sound, at the top of the left temporal lobe, under your temple. That strip is tuned to exactly that slow, rough change. The more neatly its nerve cells were arranged, the better the person read. That link was partly genetic.

Second, sharpen it. Rough syllables are not enough. You need the fine differences between speech sounds, and that is the primary auditory cortex's own job. There a thicker cortex — the brain's outer layer — went with better reading, but showed no genetic signal. Listening and reading practice may be what thickens it.

Third, see the shape. Skilled readers take a printed word in directly, not only by sounding it out. We break letters into bows, dots and lines much as we break a face into eyes, nose and chin. So it fits that the area used to identify faces, on the right side, was larger in better readers. That link ran in families too.

Fourth, meaning. A region at the front of the left temporal lobe ties word form to meaning. Bigger meant quicker access to meaning, and this was inherited as well.

Then the wiring. The nerve fibre bundles joining sound, shape and meaning also tracked reading skill — and these showed no genetic signal at all. They look like something built by use.

That is the pattern. You inherit part of the starting kit and build the rest by reading. Roll's image is a lump of clay you are partly handed and keep shaping. Because the clay differs, one person finds sounding out easy while another gets to meaning fast — a spread that runs across the whole population, not a line with dyslexia on one side of it.

Now the boundary. Roll once talked with a physics professor who has dyslexia. The man could not sound words out easily and heard nothing in his head while reading, yet he understood text well. He described written words silently building systems of meaning, and felt the style suited his work. Roll's guess is that with the sound route weak, that brain leaned harder on the direct road from shape to meaning. Deaf readers lean the same way; people blind from early life read Braille using parts of the brain meant for sight. But none of this makes dyslexia a gift. Trouble with the sound structure of language is a commonly cited factor in it, and for most people it means a hard struggle — that professor's skill did not come cheap either.

sections.label: The caveat
sections.text: This is one study, and it only matches brain measurements to test scores. So it cannot show that a thicker cortex causes better reading, rather than years of reading thickening the cortex. Nobody read while being scanned. The scans came from healthy young adults, so the picture may not hold for children still learning. And the physics professor is a single conversation — Roll is clear that his explanation of that brain is a guess.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: Nobody is born a reader. The part of the network that matters most is the part you lay down yourself.

recall.q: Some brain features linked to reading skill turned out to be inherited and some did not. Which fell on each side, and what does that split suggest?
recall.a: The starting parts were partly inherited: the syllable-tracking strip beside the auditory cortex, the face-recognition area used for word shapes, and the region that links form to meaning. The thickness of the primary auditory cortex and the fibre bundles joining sound, shape and meaning showed no genetic signal — which fits them being built by practice. You inherit some of the equipment; the connections come from reading.

cards.title: The most-cited AI skeptic's predictions, scored
cards.body: Someone scored Ed Zitron's public predictions against what actually happened. The companies he called dying kept growing in revenue and profit. The spreadsheet behind one of his revenue projections had a February 30 in it. A bad record alone proves little — but here the reasoning breaks in the same places.

sections.text:
The scorer has no stake in AI beyond index funds. Four calls, scored:

1. The dying-giants call missed. In a November 2024 talk, Zitron said Meta was a dying company, and that Google and Microsoft had run out of ways to grow, so they were pushing AI everywhere out of desperation. Revenue and profit at all three kept climbing.

2. The frozen-AI call missed too. In December 2024 he said AI products had been "trapped in amber" for over a year. In January 2026 he said models worked no better than a year before.

3. The evidence under the calls was thin. The Facebook decline he cited came from an outside traffic estimator, not from Meta's own reported numbers, which show no lasting drop.

4. The oddest miss was arithmetic. Timothy B. Lee checked the spreadsheet behind Zitron's estimate of Anthropic's revenue: one ten-day stretch counted twice, other stretches skipped, and a row dated February 30.

sections.label: The numbers
items: $3.6 billion — Zitron's own figure for Anthropic's 2025 revenue, offered as a sign something was wrong. It adds up once the date errors are fixed.
3 — companies written off in a single talk. All three grew.
December 2024 to January 2026 — the stretch over which he kept saying AI had stopped improving.

sections.label: Why it matters
sections.text: A hit rate on its own settles little. A forecaster can be wrong for good reasons, or right by luck. What makes this scorecard unusual is that both halves fail together: the calls missed, and the numbers cited do not support the claims built on them. That matters, because Zitron is cited mainly as the person who checked the numbers.

recall.q: A bad prediction record on its own proves little. What second finding does this scorecard rest on?
recall.a: That the numbers behind the calls fail too. The Facebook decline came from an outside traffic estimator rather than Meta's own reported figures, and the Anthropic revenue spreadsheet counted one ten-day stretch twice, skipped others, and carried a row dated February 30.

cards.title: Why psychiatry has no blood test, from inside the DSM
cards.body: No psychiatric condition has a scientifically valid biomarker — no blood test, no scan. One exception arrived in March 2025. A member of the committee planning the next DSM explains what biology can offer now, and why hunting one measure for one diagnosis may be the wrong hope.

sections.text:
A blood sample tells a doctor whether your diabetes is under control. A cholesterol number puts a figure on heart risk. A scan measures a tumour to the millimetre. Sit down with a psychiatrist and there is no equivalent. No test, no number — only questions, and your answers.

Anand Kumar spent two years trying to change that. From May 2024 to August 2026 he sat on the strategic committee of the DSM — the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, the book doctors worldwide use to diagnose patients and researchers use to shape studies. His subcommittee had one job: bring in brain biology. In its whole history the DSM has never used biology to diagnose anyone. The next edition means to start.

The committee had to work with a difference that sounds small and is not. A biological factor is something in the body — genetic, chemical, physical — that may drive an illness but cannot yet be measured in a lab. A biomarker can be measured, and used to judge a disease or a treatment. Right now no psychiatric condition has a scientifically valid biomarker. One exception exists, and it is new.

Alzheimer's used to be confirmed by history, examination, and finally by two damaged proteins — amyloid and tau — found in the brain after death. In March 2025 the FDA approved a blood test that spots certain forms of those proteins in a living person. It is the first biomarker for a disorder of both brain and behaviour.

Two more findings are close. About 30% of people with depression carry high levels of C-reactive protein — CRP, a molecule the liver makes after injury or infection. That may mark a real subgroup, one that answers better to some treatments than low-CRP patients do. Many risk genes have also been tied to mental disorders. Risk genes are not disease genes: they raise the odds, they do not cause the illness. Each adds a little, so they can be summed into a polygenic risk score — one estimate of inherited risk. Neither is ready for the clinic. Neither is nothing.

Then the wall. Psychiatric conditions are not separate diseases. They are syndromes — clusters of signs and symptoms that overlap. Anxiety and mood disorders share so much that one patient often fits both at once. So do schizophrenia and bipolar disorder with psychosis. They overlap because they share genes and environments. Worse, depression and schizophrenia each probably hold several subgroups that look alike from outside but develop in different ways. Hunting one marker for all that is not just hard. It is unrealistic.

Medicine has been here before. Tuberculosis, cancer and diabetes were clusters of symptoms first and causes second. Psychiatry has not reached that turn.

sections.label: What no one can do yet
sections.text: The biological changes behind mental illness are small, and today's tools cannot catch them easily. Family history and trauma are among the strongest risk factors for major mental disorders, so biology and life stay tangled and cannot be pulled apart cleanly. And nobody can yet say which subgroup of depression a patient belongs to — exactly what a useful test would have to do.

sections.label: Where it's contested
sections.text:
DSM-5, published in 2013, drew hard criticism from clinicians and researchers: with no objective measures, it can turn ordinary human pain into a diagnosis, and it weakens the labels it hands out. Kumar does not deny the gap. He defends the book on other ground — as a shared language for clinicians supporting patients through long illness.

How fast biology should enter is its own argument. Eric Kandel, who won a Nobel for work on memory, called the biological basis of mind the "last frontier of the biological sciences", solvable only by joining cell biology to psychology. In 2013 the journal Current Psychiatry polled its online visitors; its editor Henry Nasrallah found 65% expected DSM-6 to carry lab tests for diagnosis. Thirteen years on there are none. Kumar's committee chose caution: biology enters as factors, one finding at a time, not as a menu of tests.

sections.label: How we'd find out
items: Split depression trials by CRP. Give high-CRP and low-CRP patients the same treatments and see whether the predicted gap in response actually appears.
Test polygenic risk scores in real clinics, next to the usual history of a patient's life and family — and check whether they change a diagnosis or a prescription for the better.
Stop hunting one marker per label. The Alzheimer's test worked because it aimed at two specific proteins, not at a syndrome.
Read the next DSM when it arrives. Whether biology shows up as measurable tests or only as listed factors is the honest scoreboard.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: The missing blood test is not only a technology problem. Psychiatry does not yet know what it would be measuring.

recall.q: Psychiatry's lack of a diagnostic blood test is usually blamed on technology being too crude. What deeper problem does the piece point to?
recall.a: Psychiatric diagnoses are syndromes — overlapping clusters of symptoms, not separate diseases. Depression and schizophrenia each probably hold several subgroups that look alike from outside but develop in different ways, so no single marker could track a whole label. The measurement problem sits downstream of a definition problem.
